items.title: Getting started with apitofsim
items.text: This is the documentation for apitofsim, a simulation of cluster fragmentation in an Atmospheric Pressure interface Time of Flight Mass Spectrometer (APi-ToF MS). This page will help you get started with installation and usage. For more information about the package itself, please refer to the Background page.

items.title: Installation
items.text: This package can be installed using packages from Conda or pip (wheel) or from source

items.title: Installation using pip
items.text:
The wheel includes the native Parquet writer and bundles its Arrow and Parquet libraries. Python event readers use PyArrow. The macOS arm64 wheel requires macOS 12 or later.

Visit the release page and find the appropriate release ending .whl for your platform, right click and copy the link address. Then run the following command in your terminal, replacing <link> with the copied link:

pip install <link>

Or using uv:

uv tool install <link>

items.title: Installation using Conda
items.text:
You can also install this package using Conda. First download miniforge and then run:

conda install -c https://prefix.dev/vilma apitofsim

items.title: Build from source
items.text: It is also possible to build from source.

items.title: Usage
items.text: There are two main entry points to running the simulation: the command line tools and a Python library. Basic functionality is available in both, but the Python API allows for more customization.

items.title: Using apitofsim from the command line
items.text: First, refer to the guide which walks through using all major features of the package through the command line. Next, you can refer to the reference for the command line tools and for the configuration files.

items.title: Using apitofsim from Python
items.text: See the reference documentation.

items.title: Background on the APi-TOF simulation
items.text: This page gives some background information on how the package works and gives references to relevant publications at a high level. For a more detailed, self-contained mathematical description, see Simulation model and numerical methods (PDF).

items.title: How does it work?
items.text: The simulation runs a number of iterations with each one considering a single instance of a cluster travelling through an APi-TOF MS. The main simulation loop considers the distributions of the time until the next collision between the cluster and a gas molecule, the speed/angle of that collision, and the time until the cluster fragments. The main quantity of interest is the probability the cluster survives to reach the detector --- currently modelled as simply reaching the end of the instrument --- without fragmenting.

items.title: Publications describing the simulation
items.text:
The main principles of the simulation are described across a number of publications.

Zapadinsky et al. (2019)1 describe the simplest version of the simulation, in which only a single pressure and electric field are considered. Further information on the equations are given in the supporting information2. The main parts described are the overall scheme of simulation. The actual code used for this publication was written in Matlab and is not publicly available.

Zanca et al. (2020)3 describe a version of the simulation expanding the above to consider five zones. Zone I being the first chamber, II the skimmer, and III-V the second chamber, before, during and after the quadrupole respectively. This publication describes the simulation of the skimmer and quadrupole. The code used in this publication is an earlier version of the code in this repository.

Later, Zanca, T. (2025)4 added support for atom-like products.

The current version of the code supports sampling schemes other than the originally described histogram-based technique. The rejection sampling method is described in one of the notebooks included in the source code repository.

Three approaches to considering multiple fragmentation pathways, e.g. in order to obtain the intensities of a spectrogram, have been added. In the first and default, the simulation considers multiple pathways at once. In particular, after a collision with a gas particle, survival probability distributions are considered for all pathways, and the first to occur after sampling determines the fragmentation pathways along which the fragmentation occurs in the case that another simulated gas collision does not happen first. In the second, corresponding to earlier versions of the code, the simulation considers each pathway separately and uses assumptions of independence to obtain the overall survival probability as the product of the survival probabilities of each pathway. Beyond this, per-pathway fragmentation probabilities can be found using independence and assuming fragmentation happens in an order proportional to some measure of overall pathway fragmentation as outlined by Zanca, T. (2025)5. This second approach is available through the --simulation-mode=pathway-at-a-time option. A final is the cluster tree approach which carries on simulating charged daughter ions after fragmentation, and is available through the --simulation-mode=cluster-tree option. This is described in Simulation model and numerical methods (PDF).

The software has some additional features not yet described in publication or via a notebook, although they are covered in Simulation model and numerical methods (PDF). They are:

  • Support for either negatively or positively charged clusters.
  • Pinhole rejection: Extra code to compensate for reduced gas collision frequency near to the pinhole.
  • Modelling of the skimmer using a quasi-one-dimensional isentropic nozzle flow calculation.

items.title: Publications using the simulation
items.text:
These publications make use of (previous versions of) this simulation:

  • Alfaouri et al. (2022)6 used an older version of the code, without support for the quadrupole, pinhole rejection or multiple fragmentation pathways. In this publication, the overall rejection rate is obtained as the product of the rejection rate of individual pathways. The workflow example builds on this study.

  1. Zapadinsky, E., Passananti, M., Myllys, N., Kurtén, T., & Vehkamäki, H. (2019). Modeling on Fragmentation of Clusters inside a Mass Spectrometer. The Journal of Physical Chemistry. A, 123, 611 - 624. [web] [pdf] [doi] ↩

  2. Zapadinsky, E., Passananti, M., Myllys, N., Kurtén, T., & Vehkamäki, H. (2019). Supporting Information to "Modelling on Fragmentation of Clusters Inside a Mass Spectrometer" [pdf] ↩

  3. Zanca, T., Kubečka, J., Zapadinsky, E., Passananti, M., Kurtén, T., & Vehkamäki, H. (2020). Highly oxygenated organic molecule cluster decomposition in atmospheric pressure interface time-of-flight mass spectrometers. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 13, 3581-3593. [web] [pdf] [doi] ↩

  4. Zanca, T. (2025). Fragmentation rate constant for an atom-like product. Note published online. [web] ↩

  5. Zanca, T. (2025). Single and multi-pathway fragmentations. Note published online. [web] ↩

  6. Alfaouri, D., Passananti, M., Zanca, T., Ahonen, L., Kangasluoma, J., Kubečka, J., Myllys, N., and Vehkamäki, H. (2022). A study on the fragmentation of sulfuric acid and dimethylamine clusters inside an atmospheric pressure interface time-of-flight mass spectrometer. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 15, 11–19. [web] [pdf] [doi] ↩

items.title: apitofsim db prepare
items.text:
Prepare the database according to MODE at path DATABASE using the json configuration file at path CONFIG.

Typically, you will be creating an database in order to run simulation experiments, and so --db-type should be kept as --db-type=experiment.

MODE can be create or append, depending on whether you want to create a new database or append to an existing one.

You may choose to --warm your database, so that histogramming is done now, in advance of the simulation itself.

The CONFIG file specifies a TOML formatted file containing both where to import the information about the cluster and pathways from, and the parameters to use for the simulation.

Pathways For pathways, you can specify the type as "legacy_glob" or "csv".

The "legacy_glob" type imports pathways from the legacy .in files matching a glob pattern. The per-cluster data is then taken either from .dat files specified in the .in file or ORCA or Gaussian outputs files next to the .in file.

[[pathways]]
type = "legacy_glob"
# An optional prefix to add to the common names of all clusters imported here
prefix = ""
# A glob pattern to use to find .in files.
# The wildcard * matches any number of characters, while ** can span directories.
path = "/path/to/**/*.in"
# Paths specified in the .in files are relative to the .in file directory.
cwd = "."
[pathways.clusters]
# By default, all attributes are taken from the gaussian source
default_source = "gaussian"
# Individual attributes can be taken from different sources and combined
# using simple expressions. Here, the electronic energy is taken as the
# sum of the final single point energy from orca and the zero point energy
# from gaussian.
electronic_energy = "orca.final_single_point_energy + gaussian.zero_point_energy"
# Here the sources for cluster information are specified.
# The dat source is actually unused in this example
[pathways.clusters.sources.dat]
# The ORCA source is only used for part of the electronic energy
[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
# append_to_common_prefix means that the common name of the cluster will
# be taken as the .in file name with .out appended
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"
# Finally, the Gaussian source, where most attributes are taken from is specified
[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]
append_to_common_prefix = ".log"

For the "csv" type, you specify the pathways and clusters in separate CSV files, with, as above, the information about how to combine sources specified in the toml config file.

[[pathways]]
type = "csv"
pathways_path = "pathways.csv"
clusters_path = "clusters.csv"
# These are the same as legacy_glob, see above
[pathways.clusters]
default_source = "gaussian"
electronic_energy = "orca.final_single_point_energy + gaussian.zero_point_energy"
[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"
[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]
append_to_common_prefix = ".log"

Then clusters.csv associates filename prefixes with common names for clusters: 

name,prefix
1A_1SA_negative,negative/1A_1SA
1A_2SA_negative,negative/1A_2SA

While pathways.csv relates the parent clusters to their products for each pathway: 

parent,product1,product2
2A_2SA_negative,1A_1SA_negative,1A_1SA_neutral
2A_3SA_negative,1A_1SA_negative,1A_2SA_neutral

Note that apitofsim generate pathways can be used to generate these CSV files from a directory of QC output files. They can then be edited, e.g. with Excel, to remove unwanted clusters and pathways.

Parameters

For the simulation parameters, you can specify one or more [[configs]] sections, each with a name field and the values of all parameters. You can put common parameters in the default_config section, so that each [[configs]] section inherits these as overridable defaults.

[default_config]
T = "300.0 kelvin"
alpha_factor = "0.25 halfturn"
dc = "0.0005 meter"
lengths = [ [ 0.001, 0.00244, 0.101, 0.00448, 0.0005 ], "meter" ]
pressures = [ [ 194.0, 3.88 ], "pascal"]
voltages = [ [ -19, -9, -7, -6, 11 ], "volt" ]
[default_config.simulation]
M_iter = 1_000
N = 1_000
N_iter = 1_000
bin_width = "1.0 kelvin"
energy_max = "2.0e5 kelvin"
energy_max_rate = "1.0e5 kelvin"
resolution = 1_000
tolerance = 1e-8
simulation_mode = "single-cluster"
fragmentation_state_method = "zero"
sample_mode = "rejection"
vib_energy_sampler = "dos-only"
use_old_dos_impl = false
k_total_mesh_mode = "compute_mesh_linear"
k_rate_cancellation = true
[default_config.gas]
radius = "1.84e-10 meter"
mass = "4.65e-26 kilogram"
adiabatic_index = 1.4
[[configs]]
name = "simple"
[[configs]]
name = "with-quadrupole-and-pinhole"
radius_pinhole = "1 mm"
[configs.quadrupole]
dc_field = "0.0 volt"
ac_field = "200.0 volt"
radiofrequency = "1.3e6 Hz"
r_quadrupole = "6.0e-3 meter"

Usage:

apitofsim db prepare [OPTIONS] {create|append} CONFIG DATABASE

Options:

items.title: apitofsim db report
items.text:
Produce a report REPORT_TYPE from the database at path DATABASE and write it to CSV at path CSVOUT.

All databases have the following reports * The cluster-report contains one row per parent cluster. * The pathway-report contains the input pathways giving one row per pathway, with no information about results.

Databases created as --db-type=experiment additionally have the following reports: * The experiment-pathway-report contains one row per pathway / experiment run, and includes the outcome of that run for that pathway. * The experiment-cluster-report per parent cluster / experiment run, and includes the summarises information results from its pathways. * The experiment-summary contains one row per experiment run, and summarizes the outcomes across all pathways for that run. * The spectrogram report contains the same data used to plot spectograms.

Usage:

apitofsim db report [OPTIONS] [cluster-report|pathway-report|experiment-
                    pathway-report|experiment-cluster-report|experiment-
                    summary|spectrogram|event-report] DATABASE CSVOUT

Options:

  --help  Show this message and exit.

items.title: Native event recording
items.text:
Use an experiment database for both summary-only and recorded runs:

apitofsim db prepare create config.toml database.duckdb
apitofsim db run database.duckdb --record-events

Recording appends natively to database.events.arrow. The optional ASE sidecar is database.ase.sqlite.db. Move the files together with matching basenames. --no-record-events is the default. The former --db-type=realization schema and relational event inserts are removed; old event databases require migration. Do not read the event sidecar while an append transaction is active.

Use the native Apache C++ Parquet writer to record directly to database.events.parquet.

apitofsim db run database.duckdb --record-events --event-format parquet \
    --event-compression zstd --parquet-column-workers 4

Parquet recording starts in a database without recorded events and publishes one immutable sidecar for the selected configurations. Page compression defaults to none, and the column worker count defaults to one. Readers automatically open the format selected by the database.

items.title: Event plots
items.text:
apitofsim db plot plot-events results.db plots/ writes one Matplotlib figure per recorded parent cluster, containing the instrument schematic, stacked cumulative fragmentation/escape fractions, and regional fragmentation/escape bars. Repeat --panel to select 1–3 distinct panels in top-to-bottom order:

apitofsim db plot plot-events results.db plots/ --panel bars --panel schematic --panel cumulative
apitofsim db plot plot-events results.db plots/ --panel cumulative --rescale none

--rescale schematic (the default) uses the explorer's chamber widths; equal gives each region equal width, and none uses physical distances in mm. Fractions include all recorded realizations in the denominator. Incomplete or ambiguous histories contribute to neither fragmentation nor escape counts. The former --plot-type scatter, swarm, strip and violin options are replaced by --panel.

In Python, the same ordered selection is available as plot_events_cluster(db, run_id, False, cluster_id, panels=("bars", "cumulative")) from apitofsim.plotting.events. It returns a Matplotlib figure; plot_events_experiment() yields (parent_name, figure) pairs for a run.

items.title: The legacy tools
items.text:
These tools are not recommended for new users, and kept available to support existing workflows.

If you have installed via Conda, and activated the relevant environment, the legacy command line tools apitofsim-skimmer, apitofsim-densityandrate and apitofsim-mass-spec should be installed and in your path. If you have compiled the sources yourself, you will need to add build/src/cli to your path for the following example to work.

An example is then available at examples/legacy_cli. First cd to that directory, and then follow the instructions in the README.md file, included below:

$ git clone https://github.com/VilmaLab/apitofsim.git
$ cd apitofsim/examples/legacy_cli

You can run the included example pathway like so:

apitofsim-skimmer < inputs/config.in
apitofsim-densityandrate < inputs/config.in
apitofsim-mass-spec < inputs/config.in

Or using run.sh.

Outputs are generated in work/out directory.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
This page acts as a reference for configuration files. Note that much of the same structure is used by the Python library.

Here's an example of a full configuration file used in the validation example (available in the repository at examples/validation). You will probably want to skim this, but can come back after reading the sections below.

examples/validation/config.toml
[[pathways]]
type = "legacy_glob"
prefix = "nodat_"
path = "/path/to/100DMA-100SA/Pathway*/**/*.in"
cwd = "."

[pathways.clusters]
default_source = "gaussian"
electronic_energy = "orca.final_single_point_energy + gaussian.zero_point_energy"

[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"

[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]
append_to_common_prefix = ".log"

[[pathways]]
type = "legacy_glob"
prefix = "pragdat_"
path = "/path/to/100DMA-100SA/Pathway*/**/*.in"
cwd = "."

[pathways.clusters]
default_source = "gaussian"
atomic_mass = "dat"
electronic_energy = "dat"

[pathways.clusters.sources.dat]

[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"

[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]
append_to_common_prefix = ".log"

[[pathways]]
type = "legacy_glob"
prefix = "alldat_"
path = "/path/to/100DMA-100SA/Pathway*/**/*.in"
cwd = "."

[pathways.clusters]
default_source = "dat"
charge = "orca"

[pathways.clusters.sources.dat]

[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"

[default_config]
T = "300.0 kelvin"
alpha_factor = "0.25 halfturn"
dc = "0.0005 meter"
lengths = [ [ 0.001, 0.00244, 0.101, 0.00448, 0.0005 ], "meter" ]
pressures = [ [ 194.0, 3.88 ], "pascal"]
voltages = [ [ -19, -9, -7, -6, 11 ], "volt" ]

[default_config.simulation]
M_iter = 1_000
N = 1_000
N_iter = 1_000
bin_width = "4.0 kelvin"
energy_max = "2.0e5 kelvin"
energy_max_rate = "2.0e4 kelvin"
resolution = 1_000
tolerance = 1e-8
simulation_mode = "single-cluster"
sample_mode = "rejection"
use_old_dos_impl = false
k_total_mesh_mode = "compute_mesh_linear"

[default_config.gas]
radius = "1.84e-10 meter"
mass = "4.65e-26 kilogram"
adiabatic_index = 1.4

[[configs]]
name = "original"

[[configs]]
name = "improved"

[configs.simulation]
bin_width = "1.0 kelvin"
energy_max_rate = "5.0e4 kelvin"

[[configs]]
name = "improved, quadrupole"
radius_pinhole = "1 mm"

[configs.simulation]
bin_width = "1.0 kelvin"
energy_max_rate = "1.0e5 kelvin"

[configs.quadrupole]
dc_field = "0.0 volt"
ac_field = "200.0 volt"
radiofrequency = "1.3e6 Hz"
r_quadrupole = "6.0e-3 meter"

Note there are two main things configured in this file. The first is how to ingest things, as given by one or more [[pathways]] sections. The second is how to run the simulation, as given by the [default_config] section and one or more [[configs]] sections.

items.title: Ingestion configuration
items.text: See the documentation for the apitofsim db prepare command to get started. Here some more extra reference information about type = "csv" ingestion is given.

items.title: [[pathways]]
items.text:
We can start with ingestion parameters like so:

[[pathways]]
type = "csv"
Name Description type Set to "csv" here. See the help page for apitofsim db prepare for "legacy_glob". pathways_path A path, given either as absolute or relative to the .toml to the pathways CSV clusters_path A path, given either as absolute or relative to the .toml to the clusters CSV

items.title: [[pathways.clusters]]
items.text: Next is a section [pathways.clusters] consisting firstly of top level keys referencing one or more sources by their name, each of which is specified secondly as [pathways.clusters.sources.SOURCE_NAME] where SOURCE_NAME is a name of your choice.

items.title: [pathways.clusters.sources.SOURCE_NAME]
items.text:
The SOURCE_NAME will be used as the name of a column of the clusters CSV file given by clusters_path which will contain for each cluster the location of the file to import its data from. Alternatively in case several sources have a common prefix, a prefix column can be given and each starting with the prefix can specify and extension with append_to_common_prefix.

Name Description type This can be "csv", "gaussian", "map", "orca" or "xyz". If not specified SOURCE_NAME will be used. append_to_common_prefix This is a string such as ".out" to append to the prefix column of the clusters CSV. ignore_unicode_errors This can be set to true to skip over invalid characters in poorly encoded or corrupted files

Types "csv" and "map" allow setting specific values inline, which can be useful, e.g. for overriding specific quantities. For "map" cluster names can be given as keys of [pathways.clusters.sources.SOURCE_NAME] and values can be given inline. For "csv", new columns can be added to the clusters CSV named after the corresponding "ATTRIBUTE".

items.title: [pathways.clusters.ATTRIBUTE]
items.text:
Name Description default_source The source to be used for any attributes not specified. number_of_atoms The number of atoms in the compound. This is currently only used to determine whether a compound is an atom-like product and therefore does not need to have vibrational_temperatures specified. vibrational_temperatures The vibrational temperatures of the compound. rotational_temperatures The rotational temperatures of the compound. electronic_energy The electronic energy of the compound. atomic_mass The atomic mass of the compound. charge The charge of the compound. ase Where to obtain the ASE Atoms object from the cluster to insert into an ASE database. Needed only if --ase is specified when running apitofsim db prepare.

Each of these attributes can be either as "SOURCE_NAME" or as an arithmetic expression (using Python syntax) e.g. "SOURCE_NAME.attribute1 + SOURCE_NAME.attribute2".

items.title: Simulation parameters
items.text:
For the simulation parameters, you can specify one or more [[configs]] sections, each with a name field and the values of all parameters.

You can put common parameters in the default_config section, so that each [[configs]] section inherits these as overridable defaults.

For parameters with units, a unit must be given. Internally pint is used to convert into the preferred units for the simulation, so you can specify any unit with the correct dimensions. For scalars, units can be expressed either as a string (e.g. 1.0 meter) or as an array of two elements, where the first element is the value and the second element is the unit (e.g. [1.0, "meter"]). For arrays, the second form should be used e.g. [[1.0, 2.0], "meter"].

For the following example, say we have a simulation parameters section like so:

[[configs]]
name = "myconfig"

items.title: Simulation settings
items.text:
Put numerical settings in [configs.simulation] and shared defaults in [default_config.simulation]. Each config inherits individual simulation defaults, so overriding N retains the default energy mesh and tolerances. bin_width belongs here too. The key is spelled tolerance.

[default_config.simulation]
N = 1000
energy_max = "2.0e5 kelvin"

[[configs]]
name = "example"

[configs.simulation]
N = 2000
simulation_mode = "single-cluster"
fragmentation_state_method = "zero"
sample_mode = "rejection"
vib_energy_sampler = "dos-only"
collision_time_method = "integrated-hazard"
hazard_atol = 1e-12
hazard_rtol = 1e-9
use_old_dos_impl = false
k_total_mesh_mode = "compute_mesh_linear"
k_rate_cancellation = true

Older flat files and stored databases remain readable. The Python builder and runner dictionaries retain their flat structure; nested file settings are normalized when loaded. Do not specify a setting both at top level and inside simulation.

Name Default Description simulation_mode single-cluster pathway-at-a-time, single-cluster, or cluster-tree (same spellings as the CLI flag). db run --simulation-mode overrides the config. fragmentation_state_method zero Continuing cluster-tree breakups: zero resets daughter velocity, angular velocity and vibrational energy; phase-space samples them while conserving breakup energy, linear momentum and angular momentum. Other simulation modes are unaffected. See daughter-state sampling for assumptions. sample_mode rejection rejection, dss_normalized, or dss_unnormalized. vib_energy_sampler dos-only Vibrational energy partition for collisions and rotation. Choose direct (scan), dos-only (DOS CDF rejection), or group-dos (grouped rejection with a log-mass DOS tree). Independent of the gas collision sample_mode. collision_time_method integrated-hazard Use legacy for the previous timestep-based collision clock. Independent of sample_mode. hazard_atol 1e-12 Absolute tolerance in dimensionless cumulative hazard, for integration and event location. hazard_rtol 1e-9 Relative tolerance in cumulative hazard. Both tolerances must be finite and positive. use_old_dos_impl false Use the legacy density of states implementation for uncached calculations. k_total_mesh_mode compute_mesh_linear no_mesh, compute_mesh_single_threaded, compute_mesh_diagonal_single_threaded, compute_mesh_multithreaded, compute_mesh_diagonal_multithreaded, or compute_mesh_linear (linear-time recurrence). k_rate_cancellation true Cancel intermediate DOS factors for uncached rates; false uses the previous two-stage calculation.

The default compute_mesh_linear reduces mesh preparation from quadratic to linear time while preserving the existing midpoint weights. The single-pathway API and native CLI use it too; batches avoid redundant preparation for cached inputs and atom-only pathways.

The default solver uses bounded thinning in RF fields and hazard integration elsewhere, where the hazard tolerances control integration and event location. The legacy solver ignores both tolerances and uses the chamber timesteps derived for each cluster. The workflow automatically prepares and caches RF tables for integrated-hazard simulations with nonzero AC and frequency.

The selected DOS implementation affects newly computed entries; existing DOS cache entries are reused.

Name Typical unit Description N_iter - Number of iterations to run initial grid search when performing root finding of the area-velocity equation when making histogrammed quasi-one-dimensional isentropic nozzle flow calculation for the skimmer M_iter - Number of secant steps to perform when performing root finding of the area-velocity equation when making histogrammed quasi-one-dimensional isentropic nozzle flow calculation for the skimmer tolerance - Tolerance when performing root finding of the area-velocity equation when making histogrammed quasi-one-dimensional isentropic nozzle flow calculation for the skimmer resolution - Number of points to use when histogramming across length of the skimmer region (as specified in lengths) N - Number of realizations to use in main particle simulation bin_width kelvin Bin width for histogramming density of states and k_total energy_max kelvin Maximum energy to consider when histogramming density of states. The density of states must be evaluated up to an energy equal to or greater than the sum of energy_max_rate and the maximum fragmentation energy you will simulate a pathway for. energy_max_rate kelvin Maximum energy to consider when histogramming k_total

items.title: The gas section
items.text:
For example:

[configs.gas]
radius = "1.84e-10 meter"
mass = "4.65e-26 kilogram"
adiabatic_index = 1.4
Name Typical unit Description radius meter The radius of the gas particle mass kilogram The mass of the gas particle adiabatic_index - The adiabatic index of the gas

items.title: The quadrupole section
items.text:
This section is optional. If not specified, the simulation will be run without a quadrupole.

The quadrupole force uses the current cluster's mass. In cluster-tree mode, its mass-dependent factor changes to that of the continuing product after each fragmentation. This applies to both collision-time methods.

For example:

[configs.quadrupole]
dc_field = "0.0 volt"
ac_field = "200.0 volt"
radiofrequency = "1.3e6 Hz"
r_quadrupole = "6.0e-3 meter"
Name Typical unit Description dc_field volt DC field at the quadrupole ac_field volt AC field at the quadrupole radiofrequency hertz Radio frequency r_quadrupole meter Half-distance between quadrupole rods

items.title: Building from source & development
items.text: This page includes instructions for building the source code from source, and a number of notes for debugging/profiling when developing the package.

items.title: Building from source
items.text:
Install CMake 3.28 or later, Ninja, and a C/C++20 toolchain. Bootstrap the vcpkg revision pinned in vcpkg.json, then set VCPKG_ROOT to that checkout. The following commands use Bash, including Git Bash on Windows.

export VCPKG_ROOT="$HOME/.scratch/apitofsim-vcpkg"
bash ci/setup_vcpkg.sh "$VCPKG_ROOT"

Configure and build the native executables:

cmake -S . -B builds/release -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build builds/release --parallel

The three executables are in builds/release. Use cmake --install to install them under the configured prefix. On Windows, keep the vcpkg runtime DLLs on PATH if installing the native executables outside their build directory.

For a Python source build, use Python 3.12 or later and run uv pip install . or pip install . with the same VCPKG_ROOT. Scikit-build-core invokes CMake and builds the nanobind extension with the CPython 3.12 stable ABI. The built wheel includes the native executables and generated Python type stubs.

For an installed dependency environment such as conda-forge, configure with -DAPITOFSIM_USE_VCPKG=OFF in a fresh build directory. CMake discovers Eigen, oneTBB, Arrow C++ 26, and the matching Parquet library through the environment's package prefix. For pip builds, pass -Ccmake.define.APITOFSIM_USE_VCPKG=OFF.

items.title: CMake build presets
items.text:
The shared CMake presets provide three native Clang builds, each with its own directory under builds/. All three use Ninja and treat compiler warnings as errors.

  • clang-release optimizes for the host CPU and disables assertions.
  • clang-profile uses the same optimization with debug symbols for profiling.
  • clang-debug keeps assertions enabled and builds with -O2 and debug symbols for use with GDB or LLDB.
cmake --preset clang-profile
cmake --build builds/cmake-clang-profile --parallel
./test.sh --test-dir builds/cmake-clang-profile

Use an untracked CMakeUserPresets.json to inherit a preset and customize compiler paths, the linker, or a compiler launcher such as ccache. Keep the platform-default C++ standard library to match oneTBB. For a single-threaded simulation build, include -DAPITOFSIM_MAX_PARALLELISM=1 in CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS alongside any existing flags.

items.title: Editable installation
items.text:
uv sync

Python changes are visible immediately. For C++ rebuilds on import, add the following to your local uv.toml. Replace old Meson-specific config settings and use a fresh build directory.

[config-settings]
build-dir = "builds/uvbuild"
"editable.rebuild" = "true"
"cmake.build-type" = "RelWithDebInfo"

For editable builds, set compiler choices separately from the native presets. For example, use CC=clang CXX=clang++ on the first uv sync in a fresh build directory, and use cmake.define.* entries in uv.toml for CMake options.

For clangd, symlink compile_commands.json from your build directory:

ln -sf builds/uvbuild/compile_commands.json compile_commands.json

Parallel work is scheduled by oneTBB. Applications that need a scoped limit should use oneapi::tbb::global_control or oneapi::tbb::task_arena. The single-threaded build uses the same global_control mechanism internally. OMP_NUM_THREADS has no effect. CMake enables the remaining OpenMP SIMD hints with -fopenmp-simd when supported by the compiler.

The native Python extension retains a oneTBB scheduler handle and finalizes it through Py_AtExit, before native library teardown. This also covers direct extension imports. If other scheduler users prevent finalization, it prints a native diagnostic to stderr. Unfinished simulation work still needs to complete before interpreter shutdown. Cooperative application cleanup is tracked in issue #85.

Long-running simulations cooperatively cancel on SIGINT and SIGTERM, restore the previous signal handler, and then re-raise the signal on the calling thread. SIGABRT is intentionally not intercepted and remains immediately fatal.

items.title: Using debug Python builds
items.text:
You can get Python stack traces in gdb by adding something like the following to your ~/.gdbinit file:

source /usr/share/gdb/auto-load/usr/bin/python3.12-gdb.py

You then need to build against the debug Python build like so:

uv sync -p /usr/bin/python3.12-dbg --reinstall-package apitofsim

items.title: Building docs
items.text:
The mathematical reference is written in docs/simulation-methods.tex. Install latexmk, texlive-latex-extra, and texlive-fonts-recommended, then build its PDF before building or serving the site:

bash ci/build-methods.sh

The script uses ${TMPDIR:-$HOME/.scratch}/apitofsim-methods for intermediate files (or the directory passed as its first argument) and copies the PDF to docs/simulation-methods.pdf. The generated PDF is not committed. CI builds it as the simulation-methods-pdf artifact and includes it in the deployed site.

The following will run a live-reloading Zensical server:

uv sync --group docs
uv run --group docs zensical serve

To build the static site in site/:

uv run --group docs zensical build --clean

Site settings, navigation, Markdown extensions, and watched source directories are configured in zensical.toml.

items.title: Running tests
items.text:
To build and test the C++ and Python targets together, use the project's Python environment so CTest can find pytest and the runtime dependencies:

uv sync --no-install-project
uv run --no-sync cmake -S . -B builds/test -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DAPITOFSIM_BUILD_PYTHON=ON \
  -DPython_EXECUTABLE="$PWD/.venv/bin/python"
cmake --build builds/test --parallel
./test.sh --test-dir builds/test

The C++ suite runs with one thread and again at oneTBB's default concurrency. CTest supplies the native signal helper to the Python suite. The native benchmark executables are under builds/test/test. Set APITOFSIM_BENCH_CONCURRENCY=1 to run them with a one-thread limit.

items.title: Native event storage
items.text:
The IPC recorder requires Arrow C++ 26. CMake checks for its exported arrow::ipc::internal::WriteFileFooter symbol, which the recorder uses for in-place append. The native Parquet writer is built unconditionally and requires the matching Parquet C++ package. vcpkg supplies both libraries with Zstandard support. Use matching PyArrow and Arrow C++ versions when they share one installation. Conda packages use matching conda-forge dependencies.

GitHub Release wheels link the Python extension to shared Arrow and Parquet libraries built with vcpkg. Wheel repair bundles those libraries and their runtime dependencies. The standalone C++ executables link to the simulation core. The macOS arm64 wheel requires macOS 12.

PyArrow remains a Python runtime dependency for reading and processing event data. In release wheels its version can vary independently of the bundled libraries. The release wheel tests load the native writer by itself, check both import orders with PyArrow, and exercise Zstandard and parallel column encoding.

The Parquet recorder consumes Arrow record batches directly, caps row groups at 65,536 rows, and uses level 3 for Zstandard. A worker count above one uses a private Arrow column encoder pool.

EventColumns is the common native column layout. A oneTBB pipeline assigns realization IDs, simulates histories in parallel, and delivers completed tokens through a serial output stage. Recording uses in-order output and the stage coalesces events directly into IPC batches. Final-only summaries can group realizations and reduce counters without collecting events. Python iterators use a bounded handoff for events and callbacks. The raw iterator retains its eager queue for join-before-read callers. Retained record batches own their buffers. The IPC writer borrows the event vectors for synchronous encoding.

Managed streams acquire an exclusive IPC writer lease before starting the worker. The run releases it after its last write and batch-range snapshot. An active lease prevents a second run, writer finalization, and reads of mutable writer counters. Stream shutdown discards pending Python delivery, wakes the producer, and joins it before transaction cleanup.

A database owns one event sidecar. Arrow IPC has fixed primitive fields, a schema version/archive UUID, and per-execution footer metadata. An appender verifies the previous footer, retains its batch descriptors, then replaces only the EOS/footer and adds new batches. Existing event bodies are never copied. The Parquet writer streams the same columns into a fresh .events.parquet file.

Publication uses an exclusive portable sidecar lock and a durable small journal containing the old ending and committed length. Event data, its footer and parent directory are synced before committing DuckDB's archive generation/length and execution metadata. Reopening compares generations and either retains the committed file, restores the old IPC ending, or removes an uncommitted Parquet file. Standalone files use a committed journal marker; explicit overwrite stages an atomic replacement. A journal is recovery state, not a second event store.

DuckDB keeps execution/root/tree/counter metadata. It does not insert or allocate IDs for event/realization rows. PyArrow IPC datasets and built-in Parquet scans supply temporary DuckDB event views. SQL IDs are opaque composite strings; numeric result_id, realization_index, event_index define order. Deletion is logical until explicit compaction; a schema change requires migration.

Downstream changes required before updating their dependency pins:

  • apitofsim-resultviewer must use ExperimentDatabase, transport/open the event sidecar, and sort on numeric identity components instead of opaque event IDs.
  • apitofsim-web must replace RealizationDatabase construction, pass an explicit events filename for attached/in-memory result connections, and store/download the sidecar alongside DuckDB. Shared-cluster attachments remain supported.

The old relational-event schema and EventRecorder are removed. Historical schemas fail clearly and require an explicit migration; this PR provides none.

items.title: Bumping the downstream pins
items.text:
apitofsim-web and apitofsim-resultviewer pin the wheels and the conda package of one release by URL. bump_downstream.py reads the assets and their sha256 digests from the release page and rewrites the pins in one file, pyproject.toml in the current directory by default:

cd ../apitofsim-web
../apitofsim/bump_downstream.py v0.0.18          # pyproject.toml, plus uv.lock
../apitofsim/bump_downstream.py v0.0.18 env.yaml # conda environment

A .toml file counts as a uv project, so the uv.lock next to it is rewritten as well and uv lock --check verifies both. A .yaml file is a conda environment. Add --dry-run to see the changes without writing them.

items.title: Daughter states after fragmentation
items.text:
Cluster-tree simulations can continue with a sampled charged daughter:

[default_config.simulation]
simulation_mode = "cluster-tree"
fragmentation_state_method = "phase-space"

The default, fragmentation_state_method = "zero", retains the previous reset of velocity, angular velocity and vibrational energy. The setting is saved with the experiment configuration. It only affects continuing tree transitions; terminal fragmentations and the single-cluster/pathway-at-a-time modes retain their behavior. postfragmentation events record the assigned state using the existing schema.

items.title: Model and limits
items.text:
The sampler extends the differential flux in Eqs. 35–39 of Zapadinsky et al. (2019), Modeling on Fragmentation of Clusters inside a Mass Spectrometer to the simulated parent's instantaneous angular momentum. It treats each molecular product as a spherical rotor, builds vibrational densities of states (DOS) from the existing product frequencies, and assumes an unlimited capture impact parameter, as in Eq. 39. The neutral product is sampled for conservation but is not propagated.

This is an experimental continuation model. Event times and channel probabilities still use the existing rotation-averaged rates, not rates resolved in angular momentum. Consequently the combined model is an approximation, even though each sample conserves energy and both momenta. The paper's agreement of integrated rates with a finite capture model does not validate all daughter-state distributions. The sampled velocities describe separated products, assigned instantaneously at the parent's position and time; molecular separation and torques are not resolved.

items.title: Distribution
items.text:
The mathematical reference gives the full flux derivation. The implemented sampling recipe is summarized here.

For parent velocity \(\mathbf V\), angular momentum \(\mathbf J=I_P\boldsymbol\omega_P\), and internal energy \(E\), the available product energy is \(Q=E-D_0\). The same channel threshold \(D_0\) used by the rate calculation is subtracted once. Parent laboratory kinetic energy is excluded from \(Q\). Product masses must sum to the parent mass, and the sampled daughter's inertia must match its tree payload.

Write \(I_\Sigma=I_D+I_N\), \(I_*=I_DI_N/I_\Sigma\) and \(\mu=m_Dm_N/(m_D+m_N)\). For recoil direction \(\mathbf n\), define

\[ Q_{\mathbf n}=Q-\frac{(\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf n)^2}{2I_\Sigma}, \qquad \rho_{DN}(V)=\int_0^V\rho_D(u)\rho_N(V-u)\,du. \]

The joint density of direction and total vibrational energy is

\[ p(\mathbf n,V)\,d\Omega\,dV\ \propto\ \rho_{DN}(V)(Q_{\mathbf n}-V)^{5/2}\,d\Omega\,dV, \qquad 0\le V<Q_{\mathbf n}. \]

Conditional on these, divide \(W=Q_{\mathbf n}-V\) as \((K,A,R)/W\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,3/2)\). Draw \(\mathbf e\) uniformly on the circle perpendicular to \(\mathbf n\) and \(\mathbf a\) uniformly on the sphere. Reconstruct

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\ell&=\mathbf J-(\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n +\sqrt{2I_\Sigma A}\,\mathbf e,\\ \mathbf s&=\sqrt{2I_*R}\,\mathbf a,\\ \mathbf j_D&=\frac{I_D}{I_\Sigma}(\mathbf J-\boldsymbol\ell)+\mathbf s,\\ \mathbf j_N&=\frac{I_N}{I_\Sigma}(\mathbf J-\boldsymbol\ell)-\mathbf s. \end{aligned} \]

Sample the vibrational split with weight \(\rho_D(u)\rho_N(V-u)\). The daughter receives

\[ \mathbf v_D=\mathbf V+\frac{m_N}{m_D+m_N}\sqrt{\frac{2K}{\mu}}\,\mathbf n, \qquad \boldsymbol\omega_D=\mathbf j_D/I_D, \qquad E_{v,D}=u. \]

These obey \(\mathbf j_D+\mathbf j_N+\boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf J\) and \(K+j_D^2/(2I_D)+j_N^2/(2I_N)+V=Q\), as well as linear momentum conservation. For zero parent angular momentum, integrating out \(K\) at fixed \(\widetilde K=K+A\) gives the paper's kernel \(\widetilde K\sqrt R\,\rho_{DN}(Q-\widetilde K-R)\). The transformed energy \(\widetilde K\) includes rotational energy and must not be used directly as recoil energy.

For an atom-like neutral, its spin and vibrational energy are zero. Omit \(R\) and \(\mathbf s\), use exponent \(1\) instead of \(5/2\), and use \((K,A)/W\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1)\) with \(I_\Sigma=I_D\).

items.title: Numerical implementation and API
items.text:
The sampler builds ground-inclusive Beyer–Swinehart counts on the existing DOS grid, rounding each oscillator frequency to the nearest bin. Frequencies that round to zero are rejected: reduce bin_width to resolve those modes. Counts at excitation \(i\,\Delta E\) are summed rather than integrated, so the ground state is accessible even with less than one bin of available energy. Individual and combined counts use the same recurrence, ensuring consistent vibrational splits.

The current rate DOS routine omits the all-ground-state contribution; the sampler therefore does not reuse its values. This setting changes neither those tables nor the rates computed from them. Collision sampling also retains its existing bin-centre convention. Refine bin_width when assessing convergence. All runtime energies are joules. Counts and weights are evaluated in logarithms to avoid overflow, including during DOS preparation. Out-of-range energies or missing/invalid product data raise errors; they do not silently fall back to zeroing or clip away energy.

Workflow preparation supplies both products' frequencies and the actual prepared DOS grid, including when loading cached rates. Prepared product data are immutable and shared across realizations. The per-realization random generator controls all sampling, and the rejection loop checks cooperative cancellation.

For direct Python use, construct api.FragmentationProducts(daughter, neutral, bin_width, energy_max) with ClusterData objects and Pint energy quantities (including kelvin), or bare joules. Add products=... to api.MassSpecInputFragmentationPathway, and set fragmentation_state_method=api.FragmentationStateMethod.phase_space on api.MassSpecSubstanceTreeInput. Existing calls retain the zeroing default.

items.title: Guide: from importing cluster data to spectrogram plots
items.text: This guide will take you through all the major features of the package by going through the process of importing cluster data, preparing parameters, and running the simulation through to using the simulation data to produce plots such as spectrograms.

items.title: Importing cluster data
items.text:
In the import or ingestion stage, you will prepare a database containing data about the clusters you want to simulate as well as which pathways to simulate.

Typically, you will start with an XYZ file and run either ORCA or Gaussian to generate the quantum chemistry.

The exact ORCA and Gaussian settings depend upon the material of the clusters being studied and the desired level of accuracy versus available computation time, and are somewhat beyond the scope of this guide. Sometimes multiple analyses are run to estimate different properties of the cluster, for example one which is more accurate for energetics, and one which is more accurate for vibrational and rotational frequencies. The following examples are given only as an indication of settings which have been used previously:

ORCAGaussian 
! SARC-ZORA-TZVPP ZORA DLPNO-CCSD(T) Def2-TZVPP/C TightSCF TightPNO
%pal nprocs 8
    end
%Maxcore 15000.00
%basis
        NewGTO C "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
        NewGTO N "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
        NewGTO S "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
        NewGTO O "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
        NewGTO H "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
NewGTO Cl "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
NewGTO Br "ma-ZORA-def2-TZVPP" end
end
* xyzfile -1 1 example.xyz

# wb97xd 6-31++g** Opt=verytight int=ultrafine freq

Once you have run your analysis, you should have a directory with files named after the related cluster. For example: 

2A_2SA_negative.out
2A_1SA_neutral.out
1A_1SA_negative.out
1A_1SA_neutral.out
1A_2SA_negative.out
1SA_negative.out
1A_neutral.out
Figure 1. A directory listing containing only ORCA files

It could also be, for example, that you have ORCA .out files, Gaussian .log files and XYZ .xyz like so: 

2A_2SA_negative.out
2A_2SA_negative.log
2A_2SA_negative.xyz
2A_1SA_neutral.out
2A_1SA_neutral.log
2A_1SA_neutral.xyz
1A_1SA_negative.out
1A_1SA_negative.log
1A_1SA_negative.xyz
1A_1SA_neutral.out
1A_1SA_neutral.log
1A_1SA_neutral.xyz
1A_2SA_negative.out
1A_2SA_negative.log
1A_2SA_negative.xyz
1SA_negative.out
1SA_negative.log
1SA_negative.xyz
1A_neutral.out
1A_neutral.log
1A_neutral.xyz
Figure 2. A directory listing containing XYZ, ORCA and Gaussian files

You need to create two CSV files: one to contain information about the clusters, and one to contain information about the pathways. In a moment, we'll talk about how to generate an initial version of these, so read this whole section before getting started. First however, we'll look at what's in these files.

The clusters CSV relates the cluster name to its associated files. One option if the files are named like Figure 2 is to have a single column name for the cluster name, and another column prefix for the prefix of the file name to identify which files relate to which cluster like so:

name,prefix
2A_2SA_negative,2A_2SA_negative
2A_1SA_neutral,2A_1SA_neutral

...

Another option is to have one column per source file type, and have the file name in each column like so:

name,orca,gaussian
2_2SA_negative,orca1.out,gaussian1.log
2A_1SA_neutral,orca2.out,gaussian2.log

...

when this is done, you can specify the pathways to consider in the simulation in a pathways CSV file with parent, product1 and product2 columns like so:

parent,product1,product2
2A_2SA_negative,1A_1SA_negative,1A_1SA_neutral
2A_2SA_negative,1A_2SA_negative,1A_neutral
2A_2SA_negative,1SA_negative,2A_1SA_neutral

Rather than manually writing these files, you can use the apitofsim generate pathways command to generate an initial version of these files based on the files in your directory. With the --guess-prefix option, it will truncate the file extension, assuming your files are laid out as above. The command needs only the information from an XYZ file, but can attempt to retrieve this from Gaussian or ORCA files using ASE.

So for example, if you have a directory like Figure 2 you could run:

apitofsim generate pathways --guess-prefix xyz pathways.csv clusters.csv *.xyz

And it would generate a prefix-based clusters CSV and a pathways CSV with all possible pathways based on the atom counts and charges of the clusters/molecules in the XYZ files.

Alternatively if you had a directory like Figure 1 and wanted a non-prefix based clusters.csv, you could run:

apitofsim generate pathways orca pathways.csv clusters.csv *.out

Nested directories are also supported, with the directory name being appended to the name of the cluster in order to prevent ambiguities. This combines nicely with double star globbing ** (to recursively traverse directory structures). In Bash 4+ this can be enabled with shopt -s globstar (it is enabled by default in zsh). For example:

apitofsim generate pathways --guess-prefix orca pathways.csv clusters.csv **/*.out

The next stage is typically to inspect and modify the pathways CSV in case some pathways are not wanted. This can be done with a text editor or with spreadsheet software such as Excel or LibreOffice Calc.

Once the CSV files are ready, you need to create a TOML configuration. Assuming you continue working in the same directory, and that you are working with a directory like Figure 2, and that you went with a prefix-based clusters.csv, your TOML configuration would start with something like this:

[[pathways]]
type = "csv"
pathways_path = "pathways.csv"
clusters_path = "clusters.csv"

This tells apitofsim you are using CSV ingestion and points to your pathways and clusters CSV files.

The next section tells which sources to use, how to find the filename from the prefix (if needed), and how to combine the data from different sources to get all the needed attributes of the clusters:

[pathways.clusters]
default_source = "gaussian"
electronic_energy = "orca.final_single_point_energy + gaussian.zero_point_energy"

The default_source is specified as "gaussian", meaning that unless otherwise specified, the attributes of the clusters will be taken from the Gaussian files. Each attribute from the following list of attributes can be specified either as a string specifying a single source to take the attribute from, or as an expression combining attributes from different sources:

  • rotational_temperatures
  • vibrational_temperatures
  • electronic_energy
  • atomic_mass
  • charge

Finally we specify which source to use as well as the suffix needed to get the full filename from each of the prefixes:

[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]
append_to_common_prefix = ".out"

[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]
append_to_common_prefix = ".log"

In case we were not using a prefix-based clusters.csv, we would instead specify the full filename in the clusters.csv and not need to specify the append_to_common_prefix for each source. However the sources still need to be specified like so:

[pathways.clusters.sources.orca]

[pathways.clusters.sources.gaussian]

Next are the parameters for running the simulation, the full description of which is given in the reference documentation for the configuration file. However, the example below should help with getting started:

[[configs]]
name = "myconfig"
alpha_factor = "0.25 halfturn"
T = "300.0 kelvin"
dc = "0.0005 meter"
radius_pinhole = "1 mm"
lengths = [ [ 0.001, 0.00244, 0.101, 0.00448, 0.0005 ], "meter" ]
pressures = [ [ 194.0, 3.88 ], "pascal"]
voltages = [ [ -19, -9, -7, -6, 11 ], "volt" ]

[configs.simulation]
N_iter = 1_000
M_iter = 1_000
tolerance = 1e-8
simulation_mode = "single-cluster"
sample_mode = "rejection"
use_old_dos_impl = false
k_total_mesh_mode = "compute_mesh_linear"
resolution = 1_000
N = 1_000
bin_width = "1.0 kelvin"
energy_max = "2.0e5 kelvin"
energy_max_rate = "1.0e5 kelvin"

[configs.gas]
radius = "1.84e-10 meter"
mass = "4.65e-26 kilogram"
adiabatic_index = 1.4

[configs.quadrupole]
dc_field = "0.0 volt"
ac_field = "200.0 volt"
radiofrequency = "1.3e6 Hz"
r_quadrupole = "6.0e-3 meter"

Once these are all prepared you can go ahead and create a database:

apitofsim db prepare create config.toml database.db

Foreign keys are omitted by default. Create with --foreign-keys to enable them; primary keys and other constraints remain enabled in either case. Run apitofsim db check-integrity database.db after ingestion or simulation and before using reports to detect orphan rows.

items.title: Running the simulation
items.text:
Depending on your parameters and the number of pathways, the simulation can take from minutes to hours to run. The simulation scales well with the number of CPU cores, so you can expect a significant speedup by running on a large node within a computing cluster. Everything needed is contained in the database, so if you decide to do this, it's simply a matter of installing apitofsim on the cluster and then copying over the database file.

Then you are ready to run:

apitofsim db run database.db

There are various options to the apitofsim db run command to filter what to run, however the most important option at the moment is --pathway-at-a-time which switches between two modes of operation.

  • The default mode runs the simulation parent cluster at a time. After each simulated gas collision, the possibility of fragmenting into any pathway is considered.
  • Per-pathway mode runs each pathway separately. After each simulated collision, only one pathway is considered.

items.title: Analysing the results
items.text:
All results are stored in the database.

A convenient way of inspecting your result database is to use apitofsim-resultviewer. This package offers functionality above and beyond that accessible from the command line tools. The rest of this document details working with the command line tools.

You can generate CSV reports from the database file, e.g. for usage in Excel or LibreOffice Calc, with the apitofsim db report command, for example:

apitofsim db report pathway-report database.db pathway_report.csv

apitofsim db report experiment-report database.db experiment_report.csv

apitofsim db report experiment-summary database.db experiment_summary.csv

You can also generate plots directly from the database file.

As a summary, you can plot a bar chart of the survival probability of each cluster:

apitofsim db plot survival database.db survival.png

You can also generate spectrograms. For example:

apitofsim db plot spectrogram-many database.db spectrograms

This will create a directory called spectrograms containing a spectrogram for each cluster.

Note that the fragmentation simulation does not take into account transmission efficiency. There are some rudimentary models available which can be applied in order to attempt to model transmission based on mass. These are based simple curve fitting based on experimental data. They correspond to particular instrument settings, and are expected to be even less accurate when used for other settings.

Name Charge Voltages (V) old negative \([-19, -9, -7, -6, 11]\) new_neg negative \([-19, -9, -7, -6, 11]\) new_pos positive \([25, 12, -4, -8, -17]\)

You can use these models for plotting spectrograms like so:

apitofsim db plot spectrogram-many --model-transmission=new_neg database.db spectrograms

items.title: Running the notebooks
items.text:
There are notebooks in the examples/notebooks directory.

In order to run them, first you should clone the repository using git:

$ git clone https://github.com/VilmaLab/apitofsim.git
$ cd apitofsim/examples/notebooks

These notebooks explore some of the internals of apitofsim.

  • gas-cluster-collision-sampler.py: This notebook plots the distribution of collision angle and normal velocity of the cluster and the gas, shows how the rejection sampler works, and compares it to other sampling methods.
  • dos.py: This compares different algorithms for computing the density of states (DOS) of a cluster in apitofsim.
  • fragmentation-outcome-sampler.py: Derives a conditional fragmentation sampler, loads product DOS and cluster properties from a prepared DuckDB, and explores daughter velocity, rotation and vibration with plots, SVG diagrams and conservation checks. Includes the paper's zero-angular-momentum limit and an explicitly identified fixed-angular-momentum extension.

The fragmentation notebook declares its own dependencies and can run without a native apitofsim build. From the repository root:

uvx marimo edit --sandbox examples/notebooks/fragmentation-outcome-sampler.py

It defaults to examples/besel2020/database.duckdb when present; otherwise enter the path to another prepared database. Database access is read-only.

items.title: Running the notebooks with Mamba
items.text:
The recommended way to run the notebooks is using Mamba. This will use a version of apitofsim from a package.

First install miniforge according to the instructions. Then create the environment:

 $ mamba create -p ./cenv -f env.yaml

Then you can run a notebook using:

 $ mamba run -p ./cenv marimo run gas-cluster-collision-sampler.py

items.title: Running the notebooks with UV
items.text:
You can also install the requirements for the notebooks with uv. This will compile and use the version of apitofsim you have checked out.

First install uv according to the instructions.

Assuming you have cloned apitofsim and are in the root directory:

 $ uv sync --all-groups

You can then run a notebook using:

 $ uv run marimo edit examples/notebooks/gas-cluster-collision-sampler.py

items.title: Using the Python API
items.text: This page documents the Python API. The main API is in the apitofsim.api module, most of which is re-exported from apitofsim.

items.title: Building simulation configurations
items.text:
Use build_config() for a GUI or custom runner. It returns SimulationConfig, a public TypedDict containing Pint quantities, ordered quantity arrays, Gas, and (optionally) Quadrupole. Pass it directly to ExperimentRunner or ExperimentDatabase.insert_config(); database reads reconstruct the objects and quantities. Input mappings and objects are not mutated.

CONFIG_FIELDS is a read-only mapping from canonical field names to ConfigField records. Each record exposes unit, components (an empty tuple for scalars), and default (None when no default is supplied). Object members use dotted names such as gas.radius and quadrupole.radiofrequency. Array components are:

Field Canonical unit Component order lengths meter L0, L1, L2, L3, Lsk voltages volt V0, V1, V2, V3, V4 pressures pascal first, second

The named input types are LengthComponents, VoltageComponents, PressureComponents, GasComponents, and QuadrupoleComponents. Arrays may also be supplied as a Pint quantity with the exact shape (5,), (5,), or (2,), respectively. Named mappings require every listed component and reject unknown keys. Gas and quadrupole inputs also accept existing public objects. Dimensional scalars require Pint quantities; dimensionless scalars accept plain numbers or dimensionless quantities. Values must be finite, and iteration, resolution and realization counts must be integers. Errors name the invalid field/component and expected unit or shape. Physical bounds and form-specific validation remain the consumer's responsibility.

All arguments without defaults in build_config() are required. The builder supplies no numerical tuning defaults. Omitted/None quadrupoles mean no mass filter. When a quadrupole is supplied, its frequency and rod radius are required; AC and DC voltages default to zero. Optional bonding_energy, fragmentation_energy, and radius_pinhole are omitted when None, otherwise retained in kelvin, kelvin, and meters. Histogram energies use temperature units; convert energy quantities explicitly with a Pint Boltzmann context if needed. fragmentation_energy is a pathway-at-a-time runner override; grouped preparation uses electronic-energy differences. radius_pinhole is preserved for consumers constructing MassSpectrometer directly; ExperimentRunner currently retains its existing default pinhole radius (1 mm).

Geometry follows the simulation's definitions: L0 is the first chamber length, L1 is the gap after the skimmer and before the quadrupole, L2 is the quadrupole length, L3 is the remaining second chamber length, and Lsk is the axial skimmer region length. dc is the radius at the smallest skimmer cross section. The flow calculation uses the expanding radius dc + z * tan(alpha), where alpha = alpha_factor * pi; alpha_factor is normalized to halfturn. For example, 45 degrees becomes 0.25 halfturn. This angle is the slope angle used by that formula. See configuration geometry for voltage locations and diagrams.

This example uses only public APIs; a form can substitute its submitted Pint quantities for the values below:

from pint import get_application_registry
from apitofsim import CONFIG_FIELDS, SimulationConfig, build_config
from apitofsim.workflow import ExperimentRunner

Q_ = get_application_registry().Quantity
config: SimulationConfig = build_config(
    lengths=dict(L0=Q_(1, "mm"), L1=Q_(2.44, "mm"), L2=Q_(10.1, "cm"),
                 L3=Q_(4.48, "mm"), Lsk=Q_(0.5, "mm")),
    voltages=dict(V0=Q_(-19, "V"), V1=Q_(-9, "V"), V2=Q_(-7, "V"),
                  V3=Q_(-6, "V"), V4=Q_(11, "V")),
    pressures=dict(first=Q_(194, "Pa"), second=Q_(3.88, "Pa")),
    gas=dict(radius=Q_(1.84, "angstrom"), mass=Q_(4.65e-26, "kg"),
             adiabatic_index=1.4),
    quadrupole=dict(ac_field=Q_(200, "V"), radiofrequency=Q_(1.3, "MHz"),
                    r_quadrupole=Q_(6, "mm")),
    T=Q_(300, "K"), dc=Q_(0.5, "mm"), alpha_factor=Q_(45, "degree"),
    N=1000, N_iter=1000, M_iter=1000, resolution=1000, tolerance=1e-8,
    bin_width=Q_(1, "K"), energy_max=Q_(200_000, "K"),
    energy_max_rate=Q_(100_000, "K"),
)
assert CONFIG_FIELDS["lengths"].components == ("L0", "L1", "L2", "L3", "Lsk")
# db is an existing ExperimentDatabase with clusters and pathways already ingested.
config_id = db.insert_config("custom", config)
runner = ExperimentRunner(db)
runner.start_run(config_id)
prepared = runner.prepare_from_config(config)
# Use runner.iter_mass_spec() as shown in the recording example below.

Legacy ConfigFile readers remain available. Their array ordering and units come from the canonical metadata. Gas/quadrupole construction and quantity decoding are shared with import_raw_config() and the builder; complete-input validation is specific to the builder. Stored configurations may still be partial. ConfigFile.into_json_config() preserves quadrupole settings.

def get_frequencies(self) -> Optional[numpy.ndarray]:
    frequencies1 = self.cluster1.get_frequencies()
    frequencies2 = self.cluster2.get_frequencies()
    if frequencies1 is None and frequencies2 is None:

def MassSpecInputFragmentationPathway(*args, **kwargs):
    """
    Construct a MassSpecInputFragmentationPathway
    """
    process_arg = QuantityProcessor(kwargs.get("quantities_strict", True))

    def proc_bonding_energy(bonding_energy):

items.title: Workflow interface
items.text:
The apitofsim.workflow module, contains functions to keep cluster data in a database, convenient for running scaled-up simulations.

Typically an ExperimentDatabase is created and its tables created with db.create_tables(...) and then clusters are ingested e.g. with ingest_tree(...).

After this, multiple simulations can be run using the ExperimentRunner class.

db.create_tables() omits foreign keys by default while preserving primary keys, other constraints and report views. Use db.create_tables(foreign_keys=True) to enable foreign keys when creating a database. Before using reports, call db.check_foreign_keys() to get orphan counts for violated declared relationships (an empty dictionary means none); it supports nullable/composite keys and accessible attached cluster tables.

items.title: Database read queries
items.text:
SuperClusterDatabase.available_dos_histograms_query() returns available DOS configuration IDs (histogram_params_id) and bin_width in kelvin, including both cluster and products DOS. available_rate_histograms_query() returns the same columns for configurations used by k_rate. Each configuration appears once, even when several configurations share a bin width. These are independent sets with no implied pairing or ordering; callers choose compatible configurations.

ExperimentDatabase.experiment_overview_query(experiment_run_id=None) returns the experiment_summary columns plus raw config and run_config JSON. Omit the run ID to retrieve all runs. Timestamps remain Python datetimes when fetched. experiment_clusters_query(experiment_run_id, cluster_id=None) returns rows from experiment_cluster_report, including cluster facts and is_single_pathway, optionally filtered to one cluster. Mode flags retain the report views' semantics: they indicate whether the run has single-pathway results, so a run without results has a false flag; its requested simulation mode remains in run_config.

All four methods return DuckDB relations that callers can select, filter, sort or fetch. Missing run or cluster IDs return empty relations. Display labels and date formatting belong to callers.

items.title: Event storage and read queries
items.text:
ExperimentDatabase stores configuration, tree topology, summaries and failure information. Native event payloads are stored in results.events.arrow or results.events.parquet alongside results.duckdb. The optional ASE sidecar retains its results.ase.sqlite.db naming. Move the files together with matching basenames. An archive UUID and committed length detect mismatched sidecars.

There are no physical event_info, realization, collision_event or fragmentation_event tables. event_execution contains one metadata row per execution, with its result ID, status, event count and batch range. Status is running, complete, cancelled or failed; whole-experiment status is also persisted in experiment_run.execution_status. Incomplete executions are never inserted into successful-result aggregates. The event reader uses a PyArrow IPC dataset or DuckDB's built-in Parquet scan according to the archive format.

results_query(), realizations_query(), events_query() and recorded_output_query() return DuckDB relations. Filters run_id, parent (root cluster ID) and result_id intersect. Scoped event and realization queries read only the IPC batches for matching executions or push result ID filters into the Parquet scan. Failed/cancelled executions retain their recorded events. Realization counts count observed histories, including histories interrupted before a completed-realization counter was emitted.

from apitofsim.workflow import ExperimentDatabase

with ExperimentDatabase("results.duckdb", readonly=True) as db:
    events = db.events_query(run_id=3, parent=17, sort=True).fetchdf()
    histories = db.fragmentation_histories_query(run_id=3).fetchdf()

With the optional Apache C++ writer enabled, use ExperimentDatabase("results.duckdb", recording_format="parquet", recording_compression="zstd", parquet_column_workers=4) and request record_events=True when running. A Parquet sidecar starts in a database without recorded events and is immutable after publication. Use db.recording_transaction() to group multiple runs into one sidecar. Standalone record_to= recording uses Arrow IPC. read_events() accepts either format.

Every event has numeric result_id, realization_index and event_index. The latter is monotonically increasing within one realization, including tied timestamps. These three fields are the identity; ordering between realizations is not stable. SQL's convenience event_id and realization_id are opaque colon-separated strings of their components. Sort by the numeric components, not the textual IDs. events_query(sort=True) does this automatically.

event_details, event_info, realization and event_report are temporary read views created by the database wrapper. event_details exposes position/time and velocity structs, energies, node identity and optional collision/fragmentation fields. A collision holds its before-state; postcollision holds its accepted after-state. Continuing splits similarly emit postfragmentation; terminal splits have no after-event. No event associations are inferred from timestamps.

Readers hold a shared sidecar lock. A recording transaction requires exclusive access; close other readers before appending. Event queries on the writing connection are unavailable during an append; use live Python delivery instead. Finish existing query scans before appending and do not execute retained event relations inside the recording transaction. Locks coordinate library-managed readers and writers; direct file access must follow the same rule. Deleting execution metadata hides its events without rewriting the archive. Reclaiming that space requires a future explicit compaction operation.

RealizationDatabase and the relational event writer have been removed. Old experiment/event schemas are rejected with an explicit migration message. This release does not silently migrate historical databases.

def check_foreign_keys(self) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Return violated schema FK relationships and their orphan row counts.

    Checks the canonical schema even when FKs were omitted at creation.
    Nullable keys follow SQL MATCH SIMPLE: any NULL component exempts a row.
    All schema tables must be accessible, including attached cluster tables.
    This checks declared relationships only, not simulation semantics.
    """
    # Let DuckDB interpret the canonical DDL, including composite keys.
    with duckdb.connect(config={"threads": 1}) as schema:
        schema.execute("\n".join(self.TABLES))
        constraints = schema.execute(
            """select table_name, constraint_column_names,
                      referenced_table, referenced_column_names
               from duckdb_constraints() where constraint_type = 'FOREIGN KEY'
               order by table_name, constraint_index"""
        ).fetchall()

    def quote(name):
        return '"' + name.replace('"', '""') + '"'

    violations = {}
    with transaction_scope(self.db):
        for table, columns, parent, parent_columns in constraints:
            nonnull = " and ".join(f"c.{quote(c)} is not null" for c in columns)
            match = " and ".join(
                f"c.{quote(c)} = p.{quote(p)}"
                for c, p in zip(columns, parent_columns, strict=True)
            )
            row = self.db.execute(
                f"select count(*) from {quote(table)} c where {nonnull} "
                f"and not exists (select 1 from {quote(parent)} p where {match})"
            ).fetchone()
            assert row is not None
            count = row[0]
            if count:
                key = f"{table}({', '.join(columns)}) -> {parent}({', '.join(parent_columns)})"
                violations[key] = count
    return violations

def get_all_lookups(self, parent=None, pathways=None):
    if isinstance(parent, str):
        parent = self.db.execute(
            """
            select id
            from cluster
            where common_name = ?
            """,
            (parent,),
        ).fetchone()
        if parent is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No cluster found with name {parent}")
        parent = parent[0]
    if pathways is not None:
        pathways = list(pathways)
        if (
            len(pathways) > 0
            and isinstance(pathways[0], tuple)
            and isinstance(pathways[0][0], str)
        ):
            import pyarrow as pa

            wanted_tbl = pa.table(
                list(zip(*pathways)), names=["pathway", "product1", "product2"]
            )
            pathway_common_names = self.db.sql(
                """
                select
                    p.id as pathway_id,
                    c.common_name as cluster_common_name,
                    p1.common_name as product1_common_name,
                    p2.common_name as product2_common_name,

                from pathway p
                inner join cluster c on c.id = p.cluster_id
                inner join cluster p1 on p1.id = p.product1_id
                inner join cluster p2 on p2.id = p.product2_id;
                """
            )
            pathways = (
                pathway_common_names.join(
                    self.db.from_arrow(wanted_tbl).set_alias("wanted"),
                    condition=(
                        "wanted.pathway = cluster_common_name "
                        "and ((wanted.product1 = product1_common_name and wanted.product2 = product2_common_name) "
                        "or (wanted.product1 = product2_common_name and wanted.product2 = product1_common_name))"
                    ),
                )
                .select("pathway_id")
                .to_arrow_table()["pathway_id"]
            )
    cluster_indexed, name_lookup = self.clusters_objects_indexed(
        include_name_lookup=True, parent=parent, pathways=pathways
    )
    pathway_lookup = {}
    for pathway_id, cluster_id, product1_id, product2_id in self.pathways_ids(
        parent=parent, pathways=pathways, sort=True
    ):
        pathway_lookup[pathway_id] = (cluster_id, product1_id, product2_id)

    return cluster_indexed, name_lookup, pathway_lookup

def insert_cluster(
    self,
    name,
    atomic_mass,
    charge,
    electronic_energy,
    rotational_temperatures,
    vibrational_temperatures,
    import_info=None,
    *,
    ase_id=None,
    allow_duplicates=False,
):
    if ase_id is not None and self.ase_db is None:
        raise ValueError("ASE database not initialized, cannot insert ASE molecule")
    value_names = [
        "atomic_mass",
        "charge",
        "electronic_energy",
        "rotational_temperatures",
        "vibrational_temperatures",
    ]
    values = [
        atomic_mass,
        charge,
        electronic_energy,
        rotational_temperatures,
        vibrational_temperatures,
    ]
    existing = self.db.execute(
        """
        select
            id,
            atomic_mass,
            charge,
            electronic_energy,
            rotational_temperatures,
            vibrational_temperatures
        from cluster
        where common_name = ?
        """,
        (name,),
    ).fetchone()
    if existing is not None:
        for value_name, existing_value, new_value in zip(
            value_names, existing[1:], values
        ):
            if not numpy.array_equal(existing_value, new_value):
                if not allow_duplicates:
                    raise ValueError(
                        f"Cluster with name '{name}' already exists with different {value_name}: existing={existing_value}, new={new_value}"
                    )
                if "__" in name:
                    barename, num = name.rsplit("__", 1)
                    try:
                        num = int(num)
                    except ValueError:
                        barename = name
                        num = 0
                else:
                    barename = name
                    num = 0
                return self.insert_cluster(
                    f"{barename}__{num + 1}",
                    *values,
                    import_info=import_info,
                    allow_duplicates=True,
                )
        return False, existing[0]

    id = self.db.execute(
        f"insert into cluster values (default, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, {'?' if self.ase_db is not None else ''}) returning id",
        (
            name,
            atomic_mass,
            charge,
